authors: Madalena Barata da Rocha, Antoine Mathieu Collin, Camille Reverdy
title: Competing for inputs: how the European Union can improve critical raw materials supply security
method: descriptive analysis of the 60 CRMA strategic projects (allocation vs projected demand and China import dependency; promoter-reported output as share of forecast 2030 EU demand) plus trade-data analysis (CEPII BACI) of strategic partnerships and FTA CRM provisions
outcomes: alignment of strategic projects with demand and dependencies; projected contribution to CRMA 2030 benchmarks; trade effects of partnerships
headline: Strategic projects could cover the CRMA extraction and processing targets for only five CRMs in a low-demand scenario and probably not the recycling target; project allocation shows no systematic link to import dependency on China, and strategic partnerships show no measurable trade effects yet.
summary_plain: Bruegel looked at the 60 projects the EU has labelled 'strategic' under the Act and found they are unlikely to make the EU self-sufficient by 2030 and do not target the materials where dependence on China is greatest. Trade agreements have so far done more to raise supplies to the EU.
quality: Descriptive and early; relies on unverified promoter output projections (authors warn of overstatement incentives); no counterfactual for CRMA itself.

title: Batteries Not Included: The EU's Strategic Raw Material Projects in the Global South
venue: Munich Security Analysis 2/2026, Munich Security Conference (August 2026); doi:10.47342/vzmd6856
method: structured qualitative assessment of the six CRMA strategic projects in the Global South against partner-country conditions (processing investment, technology transfer, risk absorption), with project status table
outcomes: progress and value-addition features of non-EU strategic projects
headline: Of the six CRMA strategic projects in the Global South, three are listed as delayed, and the EU is judged to be struggling to deliver processing investment, technology transfer and risk-absorption finance that partners demand.
summary_plain: The paper checks the EU's 'strategic' raw-material projects in Africa, Asia and Latin America and finds several are behind schedule and the EU is not delivering the local processing and financing support partner countries want.
period_geography: 2025-2026; Brazil, Zambia, Kazakhstan, Madagascar, Malawi, South Africa
quality: Small set of cases; qualitative assessment drawing on secondary sources and MSC meetings; no quantitative outcome measure.

title: The EU's Raw Materials Strategic Projects: First Results
venue: World Economy and International Relations (Mirovaya ekonomika i mezhdunarodnye otnosheniya), vol. 70, no. 9, pp. 36-44
method: descriptive analysis of the first-round CRMA strategic projects (type, materials, location, brownfield vs greenfield) and their links to EU trade and partnership instruments
outcomes: composition of first strategic projects; diversification of suppliers
headline: The first CRMA strategic projects favour existing or restarted operations over greenfield investment and are concentrated in countries already tied to the EU through Global Gateway, CRM partnerships and trade agreements.
summary_plain: A review of the first projects chosen under the Act finds the EU mostly picked mines and plants that already exist or are being reopened, rather than new ones, and mainly in countries it already works with.
quality: Descriptive only; no numbers in abstract; published by IMEMO (Russian Academy of Sciences institute); abstract obtained via Crossref because publisher page blocked access.

title: Strategic projects for whom? Challenges and local realities of the European Union's strategic mineral projects
method: survey of the 13 promoters of non-EU strategic projects (4 responded) plus web research and the BHRC Transition Minerals Tracker allegations database
outcomes: human-rights policies, impact assessments and abuse allegations linked to strategic project promoters
headline: None of the 13 promoters of non-EU strategic projects has both a public human rights policy and a project impact assessment; only 4 of 13 answered BHRC, and at least 4 of 13 are linked to past allegations of abuse.
summary_plain: A human-rights group asked the companies behind the EU's overseas 'strategic' mining projects about their safeguards; most did not reply and none had both a human rights policy and a published impact assessment for the project.
quality: Simple descriptive audit with low response rate; campaigning perspective; does not measure on-the-ground outcomes.
interested_party: campaigning NGO on business and human rights

authors: European Commission and national CPC authorities
title: Sweep on online traders of second-hand goods (2024)
venue: European Commission, consumer protection enforcement: sweeps page
method: coordinated compliance screening (sweep) of 356 online second-hand traders by authorities of 25 Member States, Iceland and Norway
outcomes: compliance with legal guarantee of conformity, withdrawal information and green claims
headline: Of 356 online second-hand traders screened, 57% did not respect the minimum 1-year legal guarantee for second-hand goods and 45% did not correctly inform consumers about the legal guarantee of conformity.
summary_plain: National consumer authorities checked hundreds of websites selling used goods and found that more than half did not honour the minimum one-year guarantee that EU sales law allows for second-hand items.
quality: Compliance snapshot with numbers but non-random targeted sample, no pre/post comparison; covers several directives (SGD, CRD, UCPD); Commission-coordinated.
interested_party: Commission and enforcement authorities reporting on own enforcement

authors: External contractor for DG CNECT, European Commission (consortium reported as Intellera Consulting, PPMI and PwC EU Services; not named in the report)
title: Study to support the evaluation of the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) and the European Cybersecurity Certification Framework: Final Report (4 December 2024)
venue: Publications Office of the European Union; doi:10.2759/7122638
method: mixed-methods ex-post evaluation: document and monitoring data review, 65 interviews, stakeholder survey programme with 209 responses (70 on the certification framework), public consultation, two workshops
outcomes: effectiveness, efficiency, relevance, coherence, EU added value of ENISA and the certification framework
headline: Based on 65 interviews and 209 survey responses, ENISA largely met stakeholder needs, but the certification framework made slow progress (only the EUCC scheme completed adoption by 2024; EUCS and EU5G still pending) and only partially met its objectives.
summary_plain: The independent study behind the Commission's review found the EU cyber agency generally useful, but the EU-wide cybersecurity certification system set up by the Act has been slow, with only one certification scheme adopted after five years.
quality: Stakeholder-based qualitative evaluation without counterfactual; commissioned by the Commission; underpins the existing 2026 Commission evaluation report (distinct document with separate evidence base).
interested_party: commissioned by the European Commission (self-evaluation support)

authors: Christian Szedlak, Holger Reinemann, Stefan Hatzelmann
title: Ensuring cybersecurity compliance: Assessing SME awareness and preparedness for the Cyber Resilience Act
venue: Proceedings of the 5th Asia Pacific Conference on Industrial Engineering and Operations Management (IEOM), Tokyo, September 2024
method: quantitative survey: 673 responses from 416 SMEs, 160 large and 91 very large enterprises
outcomes: CRA awareness and preparedness by firm size
headline: Only 12.3% of SMEs were aware of the CRA compared with 83.5% of very large enterprises.
summary_plain: A large survey of companies found that very few small firms knew about the Cyber Resilience Act, while most very large firms did; small firms cited skills shortages and unclear rules.
quality: Large sample but self-reported awareness, sampling frame unclear from abstract, survey around adoption (before obligations apply).

authors: Roosa Risto, Mohit Sethi, Mika Katara
title: Effects of the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) on Industrial Equipment Manufacturing Companies
method: structured survey (44-question questionnaire in one-hour interviews) of 12 companies: 7 large industrial equipment manufacturers and 5 partner/consultancy firms
outcomes: anticipated CRA compliance challenges (secure development lifecycle, vulnerability notification, skills)
headline: 9 of 12 participating companies (75%) were quite or very familiar with IEC 62443-4-1 and the CRA; key anticipated hurdles were secure development practices, meeting vulnerability-notification deadlines and cybersecurity skills gaps.
summary_plain: Interviews with a dozen industrial machinery firms show they expect the hardest parts of the new cyber rules to be secure software development and reporting vulnerabilities on time.
quality: Very small convenience sample (authors note no statistical inference possible); used December 2023 text; anticipated, not realised, effects.

title: IoT & OT Cybersecurity Report 2025
outcomes: CRA familiarity, compliance measures, SBOM adoption
headline: Only 32% of 300 German industrial firms were thoroughly familiar with CRA requirements, 14% had launched extensive compliance measures, and 12% had an SBOM for all affected products.
summary_plain: A survey by a security vendor found most German industrial firms are not yet ready for the Cyber Resilience Act, with few having a full software parts list for their connected products.
quality: Vendor survey with commercial interest in CRA compliance tools; sampling method not disclosed; self-reported.
interested_party: cybersecurity compliance vendor selling CRA/SBOM tooling

authors: Adrienn Lawson (Linux Foundation); foreword by Roman Zhukov
title: 2026 CRA Awareness and Readiness: Structural Unreadiness and Stagnating Awareness for Global CRA Compliance
method: survey of 843 respondents (second wave after 2025 report) plus security analysis of over 12,000 open source projects indexed on LFX
outcomes: CRA awareness, deadline knowledge, SBOM practice, compliance expectations, private-fork costs
headline: 66% of respondents remain unfamiliar with the CRA (62% in 2025); only 34% identify December 2027 as the full compliance date; SBOMs for all products stayed at 32%, and passive reliance on upstream fixes rose from 46% to 51%.
summary_plain: A year after the first survey, most people building software still do not know the Cyber Resilience Act, and companies' preparation has barely moved.
period_geography: 2026; global, with EU and North America breakdowns
quality: Follow-up wave of the existing Lawson & Hendrick (2025) survey with new data; non-probability sample, broadened to more North American respondents, which may affect comparability.
interested_party: Linux Foundation/OpenSSF (industry-funded open source foundation); co-produced with Balena, Ericsson and Revanite

title: The impact of the Digital Content Directive on online platforms' Terms of Service
method: content analysis (qualitative and quantitative) of 100 online platform Terms of Service after the DCD became applicable
outcomes: presence of content descriptions, retrieval rights, unilateral deletion clauses in ToS
headline: 28% of 100 platform Terms of Service studied contain no description of the digital content offered, and many fail other DCD requirements such as the right to retrieve one's content.
summary_plain: Looking at 100 online platforms' terms after the Directive took effect, the authors found that over a quarter did not even describe what they supply, which weakens the Directive's core consumer right.
period_geography: 2022; platforms offering services in the EU
quality: Systematic document analysis post-application; no pre-period comparison, so cannot attribute changes to the DCD.
